paragraphs.ncert_ref: Ch 3, Motion in a Plane: projectile motion
paragraphs.meaning: A projectile has constant horizontal velocity and constant downward acceleration at the same time, and the two share one clock. Kick a ball at 20 m/s and 30 degrees and it stays up for about 2.0 s, rises 5.1 m and lands 35.3 m away. Because the vertical motion alone sets the timing, a bullet fired horizontally and a bullet dropped from the same height reach the ground together.

words.meaning: The total time a projectile stays in the air.
words.breakdown: T = 2u sin θ / g on level ground, so 20 m/s at 30 degrees gives 20/9.8, about 2.04 s.
words.trap: Horizontal speed does not change the time of flight. Only the vertical component of the launch velocity does.

words.meaning: The horizontal distance covered before the projectile returns to its launch height.
words.breakdown: R = u² sin 2θ / g, largest at 45 degrees. For 20 m/s at 30 degrees, R is about 35.3 m.
words.trap: Maximum range is at 45 degrees only on level ground. Launch from a cliff and the best angle is below 45.

words.meaning: The path of the projectile, a parabola when gravity is the only force.
words.breakdown: y = x tan θ - gx² / (2u² cos² θ).
words.trap: The curve is a shape, not a force. Nothing pushes the projectile along the parabola; only gravity acts.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M24 116h276'/><path class='d-accent' d='M44 116c30-70 70-96 110-78 44 20 60 78 92 78'/><path class='d-guide' d='M154 116V56'/><text class='d-label' x='120' y='132'>apex: vertical speed zero</text><text class='d-label' x='40' y='38'>horizontal speed never changes</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A parabolic path with a vertical guide at the highest point where the vertical velocity is zero.
paragraphs.hook: Fire a bullet horizontally and drop one at the same instant: they land together.
paragraphs.exam_note: Two launch angles that add to 90 degrees give the same range. Questions use that instead of solving the quadratic.
paragraphs.trap: At the apex the velocity is not zero, only its vertical part. The horizontal component keeps the projectile moving.

recall.q: A projectile is launched at 30 and at 60 degrees with the same speed. Their ranges are
recall.why: Range depends on sin 2θ, and sin 60 equals sin 120, so complementary angles give equal ranges.

recall.q: A ball is thrown at 20 m/s at 30 degrees. Its time of flight is about
recall.why: T is 2u sin θ / g, which is 2 times 20 times 0.5 divided by 9.8, about 2.04 s.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Ch 3, Motion in a Plane: relative velocity
paragraphs.meaning: The velocity of A seen from B is v(A) minus v(B), subtracted as vectors rather than as sizes. Rain falling at 4 m/s while you walk at 3 m/s appears to come at 5 m/s, tilted about 37 degrees from the vertical, which is why an umbrella leans forward. Two trains at 60 km/h passing in opposite directions close on each other at 120 km/h, not 60.

words.meaning: The velocity of one body measured in the frame of another.
words.breakdown: v(A relative to B) = v(A) - v(B), a vector subtraction.
words.trap: Speeds cannot simply be subtracted unless the motions are along one line. Rain and a walker meet at an angle, so 4 and 3 give 5.

words.meaning: The body and axes against which motion is measured.
words.breakdown: Changing to a frame moving at constant velocity adds the same velocity to everything and leaves relative motion unchanged.
words.trap: Only frames moving at constant velocity leave the laws of motion intact. An accelerating frame needs pseudo forces.

words.meaning: The single vector that replaces two or more vectors.
words.breakdown: For perpendicular vectors, the magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squares.
words.trap: Two equal vectors do not add to double their size unless they point the same way.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M40 40v70'/><path class='d-accent' d='M40 40l90 40'/><path class='d-guide' d='M130 80l0-40'/><text class='d-label' x='48' y='34'>rain, straight down</text><text class='d-label' x='48' y='100'>what you see while running</text><circle class='d-fill' cx='196' cy='74' r='4'/><path class='d-muted' d='M196 74l20-10M190 60l-14 22'/><text class='d-label' x='232' y='66'>add the runner's</text><text class='d-label' x='232' y='84'>velocity, get a slant</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A vertical rain vector combined with a horizontal running vector, giving a slanted apparent direction.
paragraphs.hook: The rain is not leaning. You are the one moving sideways.
paragraphs.exam_note: Rain-and-umbrella questions ask for the angle from the vertical, which is arctan(walking speed / rain speed).
paragraphs.trap: The apparent speed is the size of the difference vector, not the difference of the sizes. Four and three give five, not one.

recall.q: Rain falls at 4 m/s and you walk at 3 m/s. The rain appears to fall at
recall.why: The relative velocity is the vector difference, so its magnitude is the square root of 4 squared plus 3 squared, which is 5.

recall.q: Two 100 m trains pass in opposite directions at 10 m/s each. They clear each other in
recall.why: The closing speed is 20 m/s and the length to clear is 200 m, so the time is 10 s.

paragraphs.review_note: Verify page and line against your edition, and check the worked example against your copy.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Ch 3, Motion in a Plane: crossing a river
paragraphs.key_phrase: shortest time or shortest path, not both
paragraphs.meaning: Crossing time depends only on the component of your velocity across the river, so aiming straight across is fastest and the current carries you downstream. A 400 m river with a 5 m/s boat and a 3 m/s current takes 80 s to cross straight, with 240 m of drift, while landing directly opposite needs an upstream angle of about 37 degrees and takes 100 s.

words.meaning: How far downstream the current carries you during the crossing.
words.breakdown: Drift is current speed multiplied by crossing time, so 3 m/s for 80 s gives 240 m.
words.trap: Aiming straight across gives the shortest time and the largest drift. You cannot have both.

words.meaning: The part of a vector along a chosen direction.
words.breakdown: Only the component perpendicular to the bank shortens the crossing.
words.trap: The boat's still-water speed is not its speed over the ground. The current adds to it as a vector.

words.meaning: The boat's velocity relative to the bank.
words.breakdown: It is the vector sum of the boat's velocity in still water and the river's velocity.
words.trap: If the current is faster than the boat, landing directly opposite is impossible whatever the heading.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M20 30h280M20 120h280'/><path class='d-accent' d='M60 120V56'/><path class='d-muted' d='M60 120l70 0'/><text class='d-label' x='66' y='48'>shortest time</text><text class='d-label' x='134' y='136'>drift</text><path class='d-accent' d='M226 118l-24-58'/><text class='d-label' x='186' y='48'>aim upstream</text><text class='d-label' x='196' y='136'>lands opposite</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: Two crossings: one straight across that drifts downstream and one aimed upstream that lands opposite.
paragraphs.hook: Aiming straight across is the fastest way over and the worst way to arrive where you meant.
paragraphs.exam_note: Shortest time is width divided by boat speed. Shortest path is width divided by the square root of boat speed squared minus current speed squared.
paragraphs.trap: For the shortest path, the crossing speed is not the boat's still-water speed. Only its component across the river counts.

recall.q: To cross a river in the shortest time, the boat is aimed
recall.why: The whole boat speed then points across the river, giving the smallest possible crossing time.

recall.q: A 400 m river, boat 5 m/s, current 3 m/s. Crossing straight across takes
recall.why: Aiming straight across makes the full 5 m/s cross the river, so the time is 400 divided by 5, which is 80 s.

paragraphs.review_note: Verify page and line against your edition, and check the worked values against your copy.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Ch 3, Motion in a Plane: uniform circular motion
paragraphs.meaning: In uniform circular motion the speed stays fixed while the direction turns, so the velocity changes and there is an acceleration of v²/r pointing at the centre. A 0.5 kg stone on a 1 m string at 4 m/s needs a tension of 8 N, and it completes a circle in about 1.57 s. Cut the string and the stone leaves along the tangent, not outward from the centre.

words.meaning: The acceleration directed towards the centre of a circular path.
words.breakdown: a = v²/r. For 4 m/s on a 1 m radius, a is 16 m/s², about 1.6g.
words.trap: Centripetal force is not an extra force. It is the name for whichever real force points inward, such as tension or friction.

words.meaning: The rate of change of angle, ω = θ/t, in radians per second.
words.breakdown: v = ωr. The period is 2π/ω, so 4 m/s on 1 m gives 1.57 s.
words.trap: Every point on a rigid rotating body shares ω, but linear speed grows with distance from the axis.

words.meaning: A pseudo force that appears only in a rotating frame, pointing away from the centre.
words.breakdown: The ground frame has no outward force, only the inward one.
words.trap: A car turning a corner has friction pointing inward. Your body's inertia makes you feel pushed outward.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><circle class='d-line' cx='130' cy='76' r='44'/><circle class='d-fill' cx='174' cy='76' r='5'/><path class='d-accent' d='M174 76l-26 0M152 70l-6 6 6 6'/><path class='d-muted' d='M174 76v-30M174 46l-5 8M174 46l5 8'/><text class='d-label' x='182' y='44'>velocity</text><text class='d-label' x='100' y='50'>force to centre</text><text class='d-label' x='182' y='96'>cut the string:</text><text class='d-label' x='182' y='112'>the stone leaves along the tangent</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A body on a circular path with the inward acceleration arrow and a tangent showing where it goes if released.
paragraphs.hook: The string does not hold the stone out. It keeps pulling it away from the straight line it wants.
paragraphs.exam_note: Set whichever inward force is present equal to mv²/r. For a car on a flat road that force is friction, and on a banked road it is a component of the normal force.
paragraphs.trap: Drawing centripetal force as a separate arrow alongside tension double counts it. It is the net inward force.

recall.q: A 0.5 kg stone moves at 4 m/s on a 1 m string. The tension is
recall.why: Tension supplies mv²/r, which is 0.5 times 16 divided by 1, giving 8 N.

recall.q: Two points on a rotating disc, one at twice the radius, have linear speeds in the ratio
recall.why: Both share the same angular velocity and v = ωr, so the outer point moves twice as fast.
